title: Security and configuration
summary: ACL users with categories, key patterns and selectors, TLS setup, bind and protected-mode network exposure, the legacy rename-command note, and maxmemory with eviction and lazy-freeing policies.

blocks.body:
Security in Redis has two halves the exam tests separately: **who may do what**
(authentication plus the ACL system), and **how the instance behaves under
pressure** (memory limits, eviction, and lazy freeing). Network exposure sits
between them.

## Network exposure: bind and protected-mode

- `bind 127.0.0.1 -::1` — the default: Redis listens only on loopback. Expose
  it by adding interface addresses to `bind`, and prefer a private network.
- `protected-mode yes` — the default: when enabled and **no** password or ACL
  restricts the default user, Redis refuses external connections outright. It
  is a guardrail against an unauthenticated open instance, not an auth
  mechanism — leave auth configured even when disabling it deliberately.
- `port 0` disables the plaintext listener entirely — the standard pairing
  when serving TLS only.

## Users, categories, key patterns, passwords

The ACL system (Redis 6+) replaces the single global password with named
users. The `default` user maps to the legacy `requirepass` behavior.

```redis
ACL SETUSER app-user on >s3cret ~app:* +@read +@write -@dangerous
ACL GETUSER app-user
ACL LIST                 # all users, as rule strings
ACL CAT                  # list command categories
ACL LOG                  # rejected-command events
ACL DELUSER guest
```

Reading that rule string left to right: `on` enables the user, `>s3cret` adds
a password (stored hashed; `-s3cret` would remove it, `#<hash>` sets a
pre-hashed one, `resetpass` clears all passwords), `~app:*` is a **key
pattern** — this user touches only keys starting `app:` — and the command
rules grant whole **categories**: `+@read +@write`, minus `-@dangerous`
(which holds `FLUSHALL`, `KEYS`, `SHUTDOWN` and friends). `nopass` removes
password requirements; `reset` returns the user to its off/defaults state.

Fine-grained notes the exam probes:

- `%R~app:*` grants read-only key access, `%W~app:*` write-only — a key
  pattern can be direction-aware.
- Pub/sub channels have their own patterns: `&channel:*`.
- **Selectors** (Redis 7+) are parenthesized rule sets evaluated after the
  user's base permissions, in definition order — the mechanism behind "may
  read everything, may write only these keys":
  `(~app:cache:* +@read -@write)`.
- `aclfile /path/users.acl` externalizes user definitions from redis.conf;
  `ACL LOAD` applies changes at runtime.

## rename-command is legacy

Older hardening guides suggested `rename-command FLUSHALL ""` to hide
dangerous commands behind unknown names. It is a **legacy** practice: it breaks
tooling and drivers that expect standard names, it is obfuscation rather than
authorization, and the ACL system supersedes it. Recognize it in exam answers
as "deprecated approach — use ACL categories instead".

## TLS

Redis 6+ speaks TLS when built with `BUILD_TLS=yes`:

```text
port 0                     # disable plaintext
tls-port 6379
tls-cert-file /etc/redis/redis.crt
tls-key-file  /etc/redis/redis.key
tls-ca-cert-file /etc/redis/ca.crt
```

- By default TLS is **mutual**: clients must present a certificate signed by
  the trusted CA; `tls-auth-clients no` relaxes that.
- `tls-replication yes` puts replica connections on TLS; `tls-cluster yes`
  covers the cluster bus.
- TLS costs throughput (encryption and integrity checks per connection) — a
  legitimate answer to "why is TLS Redis slower?".

## maxmemory and eviction policies

`maxmemory` caps the dataset. Its default, `0`, means unbounded — Redis keeps
allocating until the OS starts swapping, which is precisely the failure mode
performance tuning exists to avoid. Set it below available RAM.

When the limit is hit, `maxmemory-policy` decides what happens:

| Policy | Evicts from |
| --- | --- |
| `noeviction` (default) | nothing — memory-growing writes error (OOM), reads/deletes still work |
| `allkeys-lru` | any key, least recently used first |
| `volatile-lru` | least recently used among keys *with a TTL* |
| `allkeys-lfu` | any key, least frequently used first |
| `volatile-lfu` | least frequent among TTL keys |
| `allkeys-random` / `volatile-random` | random from the whole set / TTL keys |
| `volatile-ttl` | TTL keys nearest expiry first |

Two behaviors the exam checks:

- The `volatile-*` policies degrade to `noeviction` when **no** keys have a
  TTL — a cache configured `volatile-lru` with no expiries evicts nothing and
  starts erroring.
- `allkeys-lru` suits power-law popularity (a hot subset serves most
  requests); `allkeys-lfu` suits cyclic or long-tailed access; `volatile-ttl`
  when expiry already encodes business priority.

### Approximation: maxmemory-samples

Redis's LRU and LFU are **approximations**, not per-key linked lists: eviction
picks candidates by sampling `maxmemory-samples` keys (default 5) and evicts
the "best" among them. Higher samples approximate true LRU more closely at
higher CPU cost; lower samples are cheaper but sloppier. This is why Redis
documents its LRU as "approximated LRU".

## Lazy freeing

Freeing memory can be moved off the main thread, same idea as `UNLINK` versus
`DEL`:

```text
lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes     # evictions free memory in the background
lazyfree-lazy-expire yes       # so do expirations
lazyfree-lazy-server-del yes   # implicit deletes (RENAME overwrite, etc.)
lazyfree-lazy-user-del yes     # DEL behaves like UNLINK
lazyfree-lazy-user-flush yes   # FLUSHALL/FLUSHDB run asynchronously
```

These apply to big values, where synchronous reclamation of a multi-gigabyte
structure would stall the event loop. For small values the trade is not worth
it — which is why they are opt-in.

## Exam takeaways

- `protected-mode` blocks external clients only while the default user has no
  auth configured; `bind` chooses interfaces; `port 0` plus `tls-port` is the
  TLS-only shape.
- ACL rules read as one line: user state, passwords (`>`/`-`/`#`/`resetpass`),
  key patterns (`~`, `%R~`, `%W~`), categories (`+@read -@dangerous`),
  channel patterns (`&`), and Redis 7 selectors for conditional grants.
- `rename-command` is legacy obfuscation; ACL categories are the modern answer.
- Know the full `maxmemory-policy` table, that `volatile-*` with no TTL keys
  degenerates to `noeviction`, and that LRU/LFU eviction samples
  `maxmemory-samples` keys — it is approximate by design.
- `lazyfree-*` flags move reclamation of large values off the main thread.
